title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) via Host Header in Server Action Forwarding
analysis:
A Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability exists in Next.js Server Actions when forwarding an action request to a separate worker. In `createForwardedActionResponse`, when `process.env.__NEXT_PRIVATE_ORIGIN` is unset, the application constructs the target origin for internal forwarding using `${proto}://${host.value}`, where `host.value` is derived directly from untrusted request headers `x-forwarded-host` or `host`.

- **Source**: Untrusted `Host` or `X-Forwarded-Host` request header in an incoming HTTP request.
- **Sanitization/Validation**: The CSRF check in `handleAction` only verifies that `originDomain === host.value` if the `Origin` header is provided, or passes with a warning if `Origin` is missing. Neither checks whether `host.value` belongs to the current application or is an authorized internal host.
- **Sink**: `fetch(fetchUrl, { method: 'POST', body: readableStream, headers: forwardedHeaders })` at line 210.

**Conceptual Exploit Payload**:
Send a Server Action request targeting an action hosted in another worker:
```http
POST /page-a HTTP/1.1
Host: 169.254.169.254
Next-Action: <action-id-for-page-b>
Content-Type: text/plain

payload
```
The server will issue a POST request to `https://169.254.169.254/page-b` with the client's request body and forwarded headers.

title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) via Host Header in Server Action Redirects
analysis:
A Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability exists in Next.js Server Actions when handling action redirects. In `createRedirectRenderResult`, when a Server Action redirects to an app-relative path (e.g. `redirect('/...')`), Next.js attempts to pre-fetch the flight render result from the redirected path by sending an internal `fetch` request. If `process.env.__NEXT_PRIVATE_ORIGIN` is not set, the origin is constructed as `${proto}://${originalHost.value}`, where `originalHost` is taken directly from the client's untrusted `x-forwarded-host` or `host` headers.

- **Source**: Untrusted `Host` or `X-Forwarded-Host` request header in an incoming HTTP request triggering a Server Action.
- **Sanitization/Validation**: The code only checks `isAppRelativeRedirect` (`redirectUrl.startsWith('/') || (originalHost && originalHost.value === parsedRedirectUrl.host)`). If the action redirects to any relative path (e.g., `/dashboard`), this check is satisfied. The host origin itself is never validated against an allowlist of trusted origins.
- **Sink**: `fetch(fetchUrl, { method: 'GET', headers: forwardedHeaders, ... })` at line 298.

**Conceptual Exploit Payload**:
Send a Server Action request targeting an action that triggers a relative redirect:
```http
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: internal-service.local
Origin: http://internal-service.local
Next-Action: <action-id-that-redirects>
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundary

------WebKitFormBoundary--
```
Upon action completion, Next.js calls `fetch('https://internal-service.local/redirect-path')` forwarding sensitive headers including request cookies and revalidation tokens. If the target server responds with `text/x-component`, the response body is streamed directly back to the client.

title: Reflected Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via unescaped dynamic route echo in res.send
analysis:
The API route handler in `pages/api/echo/[word].js` accepts the dynamic route parameter `req.query.word` and returns it directly via `res.send(req.query.word)`.

Data path analysis:
- Source: `req.query.word`, an untrusted HTTP request dynamic route parameter.
- Sanitization/Validation: None. No input validation, escaping, or Content-Type enforcement is applied to the input.
- Sink: `res.send()`. In Next.js API route resolution (`sendData` in `api-resolver.ts`), string arguments passed to `res.send()` do not set a `Content-Type` header (unlike JSON/objects which set `application/json`) nor is `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` attached. The response body is written directly with `res.end(stringifiedBody)`.

Conceptual Exploit Payload:
An attacker tricks a victim into visiting:
`GET /api/echo/%3Chtml%3E%3Cbody%3E%3Cscript%3Ealert(document.domain)%3C%2Fscript%3E%3C%2Fbody%3E%3C%2Fhtml%3E HTTP/1.1`
Next.js parses and decodes the dynamic route parameter `word` to `<html><body><script>alert(document.domain)</script></body></html>` and sends it back in the HTTP response body. Because no `Content-Type` header is specified, web browsers sniff the HTML payload and execute the injected JavaScript within the victim's session context, resulting in Reflected Cross-Site Scripting (XSS).

title: Path Traversal in getPostBySlug leading to Arbitrary File Read
analysis:
The `getPostBySlug` function in `examples/blog-starter/src/lib/api.ts` accepts an unvalidated `slug` parameter directly from the route parameters in `src/app/posts/[slug]/page.tsx` (`params.slug`).

Data flow:
1. Source: Untrusted HTTP request to `/posts/[slug]`, where `params.slug` is provided by the client (e.g., URL-encoded path traversal sequences like `..%2f..%2fREADME`).
2. Sanitization/Validation: Only `.replace(/\.md$/, "")` is applied to `slug`. There is no check ensuring `fullPath` remains within `postsDirectory` (no path traversal protection against `..` segments).
3. Sink: `fs.readFileSync(fullPath, "utf8")` reads the resolved path from disk and Gray-Matter parses it, after which `Post` renders the content into the HTTP response.

Conceptual Exploit Payload:
Send an HTTP GET request to:
`GET /posts/..%2f..%2f..%2fexamples%2fblog-starter%2fREADME HTTP/1.1`
Host: target-host

Because Next.js App Router has `dynamicParams: true` by default and does not restrict dynamic routes solely to `generateStaticParams`, the server executes `Post({ params: { slug: '../../README' } })`, resolving `fullPath` to `_posts/../../README.md` and exposing local markdown/text files on the server.
snippet:
const fullPath = join(postsDirectory, `${realSlug}.md`);
  const fileContents = fs.readFileSync(fullPath, "utf8");
